approachQuestion.prompt:
Longest reconciliation span. A read-only sequence contains n signed balance changes. Return the maximum length of a nonempty contiguous interval whose sum equals target, or 0 if none exists. Only the length is required.

Input: changes [2,-2,3,0,-3,3], target=3. Output: 6. Input: changes [2,2], target=1. Output: 0.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; -1000000 ≤ changes[i] ≤ 1000000; -200000000000 ≤ target ≤ 200000000000. Zeros and negative values are allowed. All totals, differences and lengths fit signed 64-bit integers. Compare methods using expected constant-time hash lookup and insertion, with amortized resizing.

Which approach handles the complete task correctly and efficiently?

options.text: Use boundary indices 0 through n and seed total 0 at boundary 0. At each boundary j after adding its element, look up total-target; if present, maximize j minus its stored index. Insert the current total only if absent.
options.feedback: For a fixed ending boundary, the earliest matching starting boundary gives the longest span. Keeping it preserves the best candidate for every later endpoint.

options.text: Use the same scan, but overwrite the index for the current total at every boundary.
options.feedback: Later duplicates erase longer candidates. With [0,0,3] and target 3, keeping only the latest zero boundary yields length 1 instead of 3.

options.text: Store frequencies of earlier totals and add the frequency of total-target to the answer; return that answer.
options.feedback: That computes the number of matching intervals, not maximum length. For [3,0], target 3, it returns 2 by coincidence; for [3,0,0], it returns 3 while [0,0,3,0] gives 6 matches but maximum length 4.

options.text: For each starting position extend all possible ending positions, maintain the sum and update the longest match.
options.feedback: It is correct, but enumerates every interval rather than retaining the earliest useful boundary for each total.

feedback.reason: Track the running total and the first boundary at which each total appeared. For each new boundary, a previous total smaller by target identifies a valid span. Use its earliest boundary to maximize length, then insert the new total only if it has never appeared.
details: Track the running total and the first boundary at which each total appeared. For each new boundary, a previous total smaller by target identifies a valid span. Use its earliest boundary to maximize length, then insert the new total only if it has never appeared.

Use the earliest matching boundary because distance is the objective. Replacing it with a later occurrence shortens future spans. Signed adjustments require prefix matching rather than positivity-based shrinking.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the method in the reveal. Choose its tightest expected-time and worst-case auxiliary-space pair. Hash operations take expected O(1) time including amortized resizing, not guaranteed worst-case constant time. Arithmetic is constant time. Exclude the read-only input and scalar output.

options.text: Expected O(n) time; O(n) auxiliary space
Worst-case O(n) time; O(n) auxiliary space
Expected O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Expected O(n²) time; O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Maintain one earliest index per prefix total during an expected-linear scan.
details: Each boundary performs a constant number of expected constant-time map operations; at most n+1 totals are stored.
Hash operations take expected O(1) time including amortized resizing, not guaranteed worst-case constant time. Arithmetic is constant time. Exclude the read-only input and scalar output.
The earliest-index map has up to n+1 entries; running state is constant. No prefix array, input copy or recursive stack is allocated.
Frequencies answer a different objective; latest indices shorten candidates. Enumeration costs O(n²) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

methodReveal.title: Retain the earliest matching boundary
methodReveal.description: Track the running total and the first boundary at which each total appeared. For each new boundary, a previous total smaller by target identifies a valid span. Use its earliest boundary to maximize length, then insert the new total only if it has never appeared.
